title: Can AI do construction takeoffs accurately enough to bid on?
description: Where AI takeoff helps estimators and where it slips: counts vs. areas, and 11 tools priced. Plus the drawing rules and a test on your own past bids.
verdict: Trust AI most on counts; re-measure areas. In a one-job study, counts matched almost exactly; areas ran low, façades worst.[^1][^2]
Your estimator checks every line and signs the bid. After award, bid mistakes are usually your loss, AI or not.[^8][^10]
Chatbots read specs well but miscount doors and windows.[^3][^4] Use them for scope and RFIs (requests for information), not quantities.
Vendors claim 94-99% accuracy but show no method.[^19][^25] Time tools on 5-10 of your past bids, checking included.
Start with one trade scope. One AI takeoff seat lists at $828 to $3,588 a year, by our math.[^27][^17]

summary: AI takes the first pass at takeoff (measuring quantities from drawings): it reads PDF plans, sets scale, counts symbols, measures areas.[^1][^2][^7] Your estimator checks every line, prices it and signs the bid.[^2][^5] Best on counts and simple areas, it slips on irregular shapes and scope the drawings don't show.[^1][^3][^40]
humanRole: Estimator: checks every AI quantity before it enters a bid, low-confidence items first. Trimble's own rule is that nothing goes into a bid until a qualified person has looked at it.[^2][^1]
Chief estimator or head of preconstruction: owns the number and signs the bid. A one-sided bid mistake is usually the bidder's loss, even on federal work.[^8][^9][^10]
Estimators keep the judgment calls: pricing, allowances for waste and weather, scope gaps and which subcontractors to use.[^5][^6]
A model worth borrowing: since 9 Mar 2026, RICS (the UK surveyors' body) requires a named, qualified person to sign off each material AI output.[^11][^12]
teamAfter: Estimators move from measuring to pricing, bid leveling (comparing subcontractor bids line by line) and risk review.[^1][^14]

Scope review gets more time. One general contractor's estimators shifted to scoping, value engineering (cheaper ways to meet the spec) and picking trade partners, per the vendor's own case study.[^29]
Some teams bid more with the same estimators. A one-estimator paving firm went from about 15 to 75 bids a month, per Beam AI's case study.[^15]
Freed hours can go to choosing which bids to chase. Only 6% of about 2,000 surveyed contractors knew and tracked their bid-hit ratio.[^16]

example.input: Illustrative, built on a published study's real numbers.[^1] A 16,000 sq ft, two-story classroom building: elevations, floor finish plan, ceiling plan and door schedule as PDFs, plus the spec book.[^1] AI sets scale, counts doors and windows, measures floors, ceilings and façades, and flags low-confidence items.[^1][^2]
example.output: Counts matched the contractor on 11 of 13 items, but one door type came back 10 against 6.[^1] Stone veneer came in 13.4% high and acoustic ceiling 11.3% low.[^1] The estimator gets a quantity list tied to sheets, plus a short re-measure list: façades and two door types.[^1]

recipes.name: 1. Specialty contractor, 1-3 estimators, repeat scopes
recipes.when: Your takeoffs are mostly counts and simple areas, on the same drawing types every bid. Counts are where AI is most reliable.[^1][^2]
flow: Chief estimator: pick one trade scope and 10 past bids with known quantities
Estimator: run a free trial on those bids (PlanSwift 14 days, Kreo 7 days, STACK free version)[^21][^18][^20]
Estimator: compare line by line and log every miss
Chief estimator: buy one seat only if it beats manual time, checking included
Estimator: check every count and re-measure flagged items
recipes.cost: By our math, one seat lists at $828 to $3,588 a year.[^27][^21][^17][^20] By our math, the top end is about 4.5% of a specialty-trade estimator's median pay of $80,330.[^5]

recipes.name: 2. Mid-size general contractor, 4-10 estimators, mixed commercial work
recipes.when: You bid often, and few contractors track their hit ratio.[^16] Errors differ in cost: a wrong high-value assembly matters more than a small missed item.[^40]
flow: Chief estimator: record time per bid and hit ratio by client type for 3 months
Head of preconstruction: shortlist 2 tools and run both on the same 3 past bids
AI: takes first-pass areas and counts
Estimators: check every line and own façades and irregular areas[^1]
Estimator: run a drawing check for missing sheets and tags, e.g. Bluebeam Max[^23]
Chief estimator: sign the bid; project manager reports actuals against the bid each quarter
recipes.cost: Kreo Business for 5 users lists at $15,000 a year, and Togal quotes 4+ users.[^18][^17] Add Bluebeam Max at $590 per user a year, and plan a 1-3 month pilot.[^23][^18]

recipes.name: 3. Overloaded team or bid surge: done for you
recipes.when: You need more bids out without learning new software, and can wait 24-72 hours for a takeoff.[^25]
flow: Estimator: send the plan set and a scope note
Vendor QA team: returns a checked takeoff[^24][^25]
Estimator: spot-check high-value lines and anything irregular
Chief estimator: price and sign the bid
recipes.cost: Civils.ai lists $90 to $270 a month for 10 to 30 takeoffs; Beam AI starts at $25,000 a year.[^24][^25] Beam's "99%+" figure covers the QA-checked output.[^25]

ownData.title: What do AI takeoff tools cost, and do they show their accuracy method?
ownData.intro: We read 11 AI takeoff vendors' pricing and product pages on 26 Nov 2026, from copies our reader tool captured 7-26 Nov. Ten publish a price. Four claim a headline accuracy figure, and none publishes the plan set or method behind it.
rows: $2,100 ($175/mo, billed yearly); the $100 tier has no AI[^18]
Free version; AI on Premium and Pro plans[^20][^48]
No figure found; says its own estimators review each takeoff[^47]
No: "97%+"; a QA team checks output[^24]
From $8,000 per trade (self-serve); $25,000 done for you[^25]
No; Flex plan has a 7-day trial[^28]
ownData.note: On-Screen Takeoff publishes no price but offers a 14-day trial.[^22] List prices only: discounts, multi-seat deals and trade packs aren't captured, and three other vendors' pages couldn't be read. The four figures measure different things, from outline fit to QA-checked output, so they aren't comparable.[^19][^25]

rules.name: AIA A201-2017, section 1.5.2
rules.status: In force where your contract uses the AIA form
rules.what: You may use the drawings and specs only for this project, not others, without the owner's and architect's written consent.[^49][^34] The architect keeps the copyright.[^35] Check whether your AI vendor trains its model on uploaded plans.

rules.name: GSA Order PBS 3490.3 CHGE 1
rules.what: Sensitive federal building drawings are CUI (controlled unclassified information): access is restricted, sending is encrypted and every recipient is logged.[^36][^37] GSA's own inspector general found 116 such files, blueprints included, overshared in Google Drive.[^38] Keep federal-job drawings out of unvetted cloud AI tools.

rules.name: FAR 14.407-4, Mistakes after award
rules.what: After award, a federal bid mistake is fixed only on clear and convincing evidence, if the contracting officer should have noticed it.[^8] Mistakes of judgment can't be recovered.[^9] Keep worksheets tied to their source sheets as evidence.

rules.name: Drennan v. Star Paving (subcontractor bids)
rules.status: State case law: California, followed in Arizona
rules.what: A subcontractor can be held to a mistaken bid that a general contractor relied on.[^10][^39] An AI miscount in a sub's bid is the sub's loss.

rules.name: RICS, Responsible use of AI in surveying practice
rules.status: In force since 9 Mar 2026 for RICS members
rules.what: Requires an AI register, a risk register, a named person's written sign-off on reliability, and telling clients first.[^11][^12] It binds only RICS members, but anyone can copy it as a template.

howToTest: Record your before numbers: estimator hours per bid (takeoff, pricing, review), bids per month, and hit ratio by count and by dollars.[^16][^40]
Pick 5-10 past bids you already checked, from one trade scope or one office. Include hard sheets: faint scans, mixed scales, addenda (bid-time drawing changes) and façades.[^40]
Have an experienced estimator set the answer key before seeing any AI output, so the software never becomes the benchmark.[^40]
Run each tool on the same sets. Time the whole job, checking and fixing included, not just processing.[^40]
Compare line by line: percent off per item, split into counts, areas and lengths, and by finish type.[^1]
Log misses, false hits and wrong-revision use. Rank them by potential cost, not by count.[^40]
Check traceability: can the estimator see the sheet and revision behind each quantity, and does the tool flag low confidence[^40][^2]?

Price the lift: hours saved times loaded estimator cost, plus extra bids times hit ratio times average margin. Use BLS median pay as a floor: $84,610 buildings, $80,330 specialty trades, $99,910 heavy civil.[^5]
Re-run the same test after every software update, so the pilot becomes your baseline.[^40]
watchOuts: Areas come in low on complex shapes: in the field study, 12 of 15 area items ran under the contractor's, façades worst.[^1] Have the estimator re-measure façades and irregular areas, and spot-check counts.[^2]

Chatbots miscount symbols: the best general models counted doors and windows exactly on under half of 120 floor plans.[^3][^4] They read drawing text well, so use ChatGPT or Claude for specs, scope letters and RFIs, not quantities.[^3]

Accuracy claims can't be checked: no vendor we checked publishes the plan set behind its figure.[^19][^25] Ties can be close: in 2023, Togal's founder was also an executive at Coastal Construction, the customer in Togal's case study.[^45][^29]

Checking can eat the savings: a fast first takeoff looks less fast once an estimator finds and fixes missed scope.[^40] Time the whole job, checking included, and start with count-heavy scopes, where the field study found counts held up.[^40][^1]

Drawings miss scope: temporary works, testing, access and logistics rarely show in geometry, yet your bid still binds you.[^40][^8][^10] Review scope against specs and addenda, and keep an exclusions list.

Drawings leak: federal building drawings can be CUI, and GSA itself overshared 116 such files through ordinary sharing settings.[^36][^38] Classify drawings at intake and read each vendor's data terms.

faq.q: Is AI takeoff accurate enough to bid on?
faq.a: Yes for counts; areas need an estimator's re-measure before you bid. In the one independent field test, counts matched almost exactly while area items ran low, worst on façades.[^1] Vendor figures of 94-99% publish no method.[^19][^25]

No: the evidence says AI changes the estimator's job, not the team. Only 2% of AI-using US firms saw AI-related employment fall, and 66% use AI only to help staff.[^13] BLS still expects about 17,600 estimator openings a year to 2035.[^5]

faq.q: Can I just use ChatGPT or Claude for takeoff?
faq.a: No for counts, yes for specs and scope. General models read drawing text up to 95% right but counted doors and windows exactly on under half of plans.[^3][^4] Prices still come from your own cost history, a core estimator task.[^6]

faq.q: What is the best AI for construction estimating?
faq.a: Togal is the pick for contractors doing their own takeoff: it is the only tool tested in an independent field study.[^1][^17] MEP trades should test Trimble, and teams wanting takeoff done for them should test Beam AI or Civils.ai.[^2][^24][^25] Confirm any pick on 5 to 10 of your own past bids.[^40]

faq.q: Is there free AI for construction estimating?
faq.a: Yes, as free versions and trials; by our math, paid AI takeoff seats list at $828 to $3,588 a year.[^27][^17] STACK has a free version and Buildxact's Go plan gives 5 free credits.[^20][^26] PlanSwift and On-Screen Takeoff offer 14-day trials, and Kreo 7 days.[^21][^22][^18]

faq.q: Can I upload project drawings to an AI tool?
faq.a: Only if your contract and the owner allow it, so check both first. AIA A201 limits drawing use to the project, and federal building drawings may be CUI.[^49][^36] This is not legal advice.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy when you bid standard scopes from PDF drawings and have no developers. Most firms buy: 76% of enterprise AI use cases are bought, not built.[^32] Bought tools reached deployment about twice as often as internal builds.[^33]
buyVsBuild.build: Build light when your edge is your own cost history: keep quantities in a takeoff tool and put your rates and checks on top.[^6] Don't build drawing-reading AI from scratch: detectors still score zero on rare symbols, and general models miscount.[^31][^3]

pickElse: You bid mostly from BIM (3D building information models): model-based quantity takeoff beats reading 2D PDFs. One automated BIM check covered 94.7% of elements at 91.5% precision.[^41]

Early budgets on barely started designs: AI can't measure what isn't drawn, so price from your own cost per square foot. AACE, the cost engineers' standards body, puts such estimates up to 30% under or 50% over.[^42]
Low bid volume: if you already win more than you can build, the on-screen takeoff you own may be enough. Bluebeam Core or Complete lists at $330 to $440 a year.[^23]
Federal or secure-site work: keep drawings in your own controlled setup with desktop takeoff such as PlanSwift, not unvetted cloud AI.[^36][^21]

offer.heading: More bids than your estimators can take off? Get a free 30-minute diagnostic
offer.body: Bring one trade scope and a few past bids. In 30 minutes you leave with the first step, a before-and-after measure, and what your estimators must check. No sales pitch.

reviews.notes: Wanted the before-and-after measure named and every step tied to a role. The first test step now says these are your before numbers; GC and MEP are spelled out; recipes name who does each step.
Stalled on trade jargon: takeoff, value engineering, addenda, AACE. Each is now defined in plain words where it first appears; F1 and QA were already explained.

Asked whether one office or one trade can pilot first, and what it does to margin. The test now picks past bids from one trade scope or one office, and a step prices the lift in dollars from hours, extra bids and margin.

The chief estimator distrusted 'trust AI on counts' when practitioners report a fixture count missing 20%, and wanted the study's limits up front. The bottom line now says trust AI most on counts and re-measure areas, names it a one-job study, and the counts watch-out adds spot checks. The study table states one job, one tool.

Steve wanted the price where he would ask for it and a clear promise for the 30 minutes. The free-AI answer now gives the paid seat range, the recipe shows a seat at about 4.5% of an estimator's pay, and the offer says what he leaves with in 30 minutes, with no sales pitch.

answers.human-role: Your estimator checks every AI quantity before it enters a bid, and your chief estimator or head of preconstruction signs the bid and owns the number[^2][^1][^8].
answers.team-after: Estimators shift from measuring to pricing, bid leveling, scope review and choosing which bids to chase[^1][^14][^29][^16]. Some teams send out more bids with the same estimators[^15].
answers.example: AI reads the plan PDFs, sets scale, counts doors and windows, measures areas, and hands the estimator a quantity list plus a short re-measure list[^1][^2]. On one real school job, counts matched on 11 of 13 items while 12 of 15 areas ran low[^1].
answers.table-1: Togal, Kreo and STACK fit estimators doing their own takeoff. PlanSwift fits desktop work; Civils.ai and Beam AI fit teams wanting a human-checked takeoff done for them[^17][^18][^20][^21][^24][^25]. Trimble fits MEP trades, and Bluebeam fits PDF markup and drawing checks[^2][^23].
answers.table-2: Independent tests show AI counts hold up while areas drift low, and general chatbots read drawing text well but miscount doors and windows[^1][^3][^4]. Only one field study exists, and it covers one job and one tool[^1].
answers.recipes: Specialty contractors with 1-3 estimators start with one seat on one trade scope. Mid-size general contractors pilot two tools; overloaded teams buy a done-for-you takeoff[^27][^17][^18][^25].
answers.own-data: By our math, most self-serve AI takeoff seats list at $828 to $3,588 a year[^27][^17]. None of the 11 vendors we checked publishes the method behind its accuracy figure[^19][^25].
answers.rules: AIA A201 section 1.5.2 limits contractors to using the drawings only for this project, and GSA's PBS 3490.3 treats sensitive federal building drawings as restricted CUI[^49][^36]. FAR 14.407-4 makes federal bid mistakes hard to fix after award[^8].
answers.benchmark: Run each tool on 5-10 past bids whose quantities your estimator already set, time the whole job with checking included, and compare line by line[^40][^1]. Rank misses by what they would cost, not by how many there are[^40].
answers.what-goes-wrong: AI takeoff goes wrong on areas of complex shapes like façades, on chatbot symbol counts, and on scope the drawings never show[^1][^3][^40]. Unchecked vendor accuracy claims and leaked drawings are the other two risks[^19][^36].
answers.something-else: Pick something else when you bid from 3D BIM models, price early designs that aren't drawn yet, have low bid volume, or work on federal or secure sites[^41][^42][^23][^36].
